entities.name: Palace Museum
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Palace Museum (故宫博物院, Gùgōng Bówùyuàn), established in 1925 within the Forbidden City of Beijing after the expulsion of the last Qing emperor Puyi, is the world's most visited museum (14.5 million visitors in 2018) and the guardian of over 1.86 million cultural relics representing the accumulated treasures of Chinese imperial civilization across five dynasties spanning 600 years. The Forbidden City itself — 980 buildings covering 720,000 square meters — is the world's largest palace complex and the best-preserved medieval imperial palace anywhere.

The Forbidden City was constructed between 1406-1420 by the Yongle Emperor of the Ming Dynasty, using 1 million workers and 100,000 artisans, with timber from Yunnan and stone from Beijing quarries. The complex served as the home and administrative center of 24 emperors — 14 Ming (1420-1644) and 10 Qing (1644-1912) — over 492 years. Its name 'Forbidden City' reflected the prohibition on ordinary citizens entering without imperial permission.

In 1933, as Japanese forces threatened Beijing, 13,427 crates of Palace Museum artifacts (approximately 600,000 objects) were secretly transported south to Shanghai, then to caves in Sichuan province, surviving the entire Sino-Japanese War (1937-1945) and Civil War. After 1949, the Nationalist government transported 2,972 crates to Taiwan (now the National Palace Museum, Taipei). The Beijing collection retains 1.86 million objects; Taipei holds 700,000. Both claim to be the 'real' Palace Museum — the same institutional, cultural, and political division that defines the China-Taiwan relationship.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Palace Museum's 1.86 million imperial relics — the accumulated treasury of Chinese civilization across 600 years — and its 14.5 million annual visitors make it the world's most visited repository of a single civilization's cultural heritage.
